\section{Introduction}
Compositions represent proportions of a whole: each coordinate is nonnegative and the coordinates sum to one. A predictive region for a composition should therefore contain a complete response vector, not merely a collection of independently plausible coordinates. The simplex constraint also changes the interpretation of distance. Absolute differences and relative differences need not identify the same departures, particularly when some components are small. Compositional analysis provides log-ratio representations for this purpose \citep{Aitchison1982,Egozcue2003}. Here the prediction target is a continuous composition observed with covariates. It is neither a discrete class label nor an unobserved probability vector inferred from multinomial counts.

claims.claim: Split-conformal prediction offers a useful separation of responsibilities: a fitted model proposes a score, and an independent calibration sample sets a threshold with a marginal coverage guarantee under exchangeability \citep{Vovk2005,Papadopoulos2002,Lei2018,AngelopoulosBates2021}. That guarantee does not select an efficient geometry, eliminate variation in coverage between groups, or survive arbitrary distribution shift. A globally calibrated residual norm can allocate too much radius to low-noise covariates and too little to high-noise covariates. A positive covariate-dependent scale is a simple way to adapt the radius without changing the calibration principle. Whether the resulting regions are preferable still depends on what is measured and where they are deployed.

claims.claim:
\paragraph{Composition and conditional scale estimation.}
Logistic-normal distributions provide a continuous model on the interior simplex \citep{AitchisonShen1980}; log-ratio analysis avoids treating constrained coordinates as unconstrained measurements \citep{Aitchison1982}. The isometric transform supplies Euclidean coordinates for relative geometry \citep{Egozcue2003}. Within that representation, our scale family combines ridge regularization \citep{HoerlKennard1970} with quantile-loss fitting \citep{KoenkerBassett1978,KoenkerHallock2001} and shallow additive updates motivated by boosting \citep{Friedman2001,Friedman2002}. Quantile regression forests are a different conditional-quantile approach \citep{Meinshausen2006}; we do not evaluate forests. Cross-validation and conservative model selection are standard tools rather than novel contributions \citep{Stone1974,Hastie2009}.

claims.claim:
\paragraph{What reliability can mean.}
Conditional-validity distinctions matter even when marginal calibration is theoretically justified \citep{Vovk2012,BarberLimits2021}. We therefore report fixed-group discrepancies without claiming distribution-free conditional coverage. Weighted conformal methods under covariate shift require additional structure \citep{Tibshirani2019}; robustness beyond exchangeability is a separate methodological problem \citep{BarberBeyond2023}. We implement neither correction. Finally, Wilson intervals and bootstrap summaries quantify different sources of empirical uncertainty \citep{Wilson1927,Efron1979}: the former describe individual coverage proportions, whereas our main comparative interval resamples independent seeds. No literature comparison is used as a substitute for a measured experimental comparison.

claims.claim: The inspected learner fits $T_i=\log\max(r_i,10^{-12})$, where $r_i$ is a training residual norm. Its reference model regresses log residuals on an intercept, standardized covariates, and their coordinatewise squares, with ridge penalty 2 on non-intercept coefficients. A second model estimates the conditional 0.9 quantile of log norms using additive decision stumps. It starts from the empirical target quantile and adds at most 80 updates with learning rate 0.1. For each covariate, 15 empirical split quantiles between 0.05 and 0.95 are considered. Each leaf must contain at least $\max(20,\lceil0.03n\rceil)$ fitting observations. The selected split minimizes mean pinball loss after its shrunken update; fitting stops when no numerical loss improvement remains.

claims.claim: Exponentiation produces positive scales. The evaluator applies the same clipping interval, $[10^{-4},10^4]$, at calibration and prediction. A constant multiplicative factor cancels between calibrated scores and region radii when clipping does not change the scale shape. Thus fitting a nominal tail level does not itself impose the final coverage level. Calibration does that independently. The recorded results do not reveal which candidate was selected in each fit; interpreting every local result as a stump result would be unsupported.

claims.claim: Reference mass is a probe-based size measure, not intrinsic simplex volume. At 128 fixed test-covariate locations, the evaluator draws 1,024 probes per location: half from a Gaussian in ILR coordinates centered at the shared fitted center and half from a uniform-simplex Dirichlet distribution. The Gaussian covariance uses residual vectors from both training partitions, with diagonal regularization 0.01. The same probes are shared by methods. The reported $M$ is the fraction of probes in the region, averaged over the nominal levels. Because the reference distribution depends on fitted quantities and mixes distinct geometries, $M$ should only be interpreted under this declared measure.

\subsection{Homoscedastic and Heteroscedastic Conditions}
Figure~\ref{fig:coverage} shows that the homoscedastic conditions provide a meaningful negative control. Mean local and global utilities are 0.85319 versus 0.85326 for H3, and 0.87887 versus 0.88028 for H10. Their mean reference masses are nearly equal: 0.55883 versus 0.55803 and 0.45106 versus 0.45105. Thus there is no consistent homoscedastic advantage to offset the complexity of learning a scale. We do not interpret these small observed differences as a precisely established disadvantage; no condition-specific inferential interval is supplied.

Reference mass also decreases, from 0.47580 to 0.39349 and from 0.49497 to 0.32211. Local mean coverage at nominal 0.90 is 0.89689 in B3 and 0.90706 in B10. These joint observations support improved allocation under the evaluated heteroscedastic mechanism, while the remaining discrepancies preclude claiming exact conditional calibration.

claims.claim: Raw-coordinate methods are useful alternatives rather than uniformly weak baselines. Bonferroni is conservative in these heteroscedastic conditions: at nominal 0.90 its mean coverage is 0.93465 in B3 and 0.93717 in B10. Its group errors are lower than global ILR's but higher than the local procedure's. Raw $L_\infty$ also improves some global-ILR summaries without matching the local procedure's aggregate tradeoff. The comparison concerns complete region constructions. It cannot separate coordinate geometry, calibration multiplicity, and learned adaptation into isolated causal contributions.

\subsection{Shift Stress Test and the Cost of Coverage Repair}
The shift exposes a substantial gap between global calibration and local scaling in the recorded data. At nominal 0.90, global ILR covers 0.74748 of responses in S3 and 0.70190 in S10; local scaling covers 0.89933 and 0.91610. At nominal 0.95 the corresponding global means are 0.85067 and 0.81405, versus local means 0.94979 and 0.95768. The raw-coordinate baselines mitigate some of this undercoverage but do not reach the same mean coverage in these conditions. This is evidence about the specified covariate shift, not evidence that ordinary split conformal becomes valid under arbitrary shift.

claims.claim: Figure~\ref{fig:mass} makes the efficiency qualification explicit. S3 local mass is 0.50795, exceeding global ILR's 0.47945. A global region that misses many shifted responses can look artificially economical. Local scaling pays additional mass while restoring empirical coverage in that condition. S10 instead has local mass 0.47159 versus global mass 0.49482. The two outcomes rule out a uniform region-size claim even within this limited evaluation. They also illustrate why mass and coverage should be inspected together rather than collapsing the interpretation into one scalar.

\subsection{Alignment Controls and Attribution Limits}
The constant-covariate control agrees with global ILR, with aggregate utility 0.82960. Permuting training residual targets gives utility 0.82985, compared with 0.87723 for aligned local scaling; the paired interval for the aligned-minus-permuted utility difference is [0.04313, 0.05109]. This comparison supports the relevance of covariate--residual alignment to the complete procedure under this design. Permutation also changes model selection and estimation, so it does not isolate a particular functional component. All declared control checks pass in the final record, which is a diagnostic result rather than a separate scientific guarantee.

claims.claim: The empirical scope is narrow: continuous, strictly positive synthetic compositions at two dimensions and two nominal levels. Exact zeros, sparse count responses, real topic proportions, and estimated class-probability vectors are not evaluated. A prediction region for the observed continuous response is not automatically a confidence region for a latent composition. Nor do the results compare label-set classification methods. Six seeds quantify repeatability only coarsely; the bootstrap cannot recover unobserved distributional diversity or correct selection biases outside the frozen final assessment.
